headline: Big 5 Day Two: The Awards Say Where Saudi Attention Has Moved
deck: Refrigerant transition, circular-economy materials and operational sustainability took the show's three Impact Trail awards. The conference agenda reads like a list of the places Saudi projects lose time.
excerpt: Big 5 Construct Saudi reached its second day at Riyadh Front with more than 1,000 exhibitors from over 50 countries and four co-located events. The Impact Trail awards went to Prime Middle East Trading Company, Masdar and Al-Futtaim Engineering.
content:
Big 5 Construct Saudi reached its second day at the Riyadh Front Exhibition & Conference Center on 31 August, midway through a four-day run under the patronage of the Ministry of Industry and Mineral Resources. The show was opened on 30 August by Eng Fawaz bin Badr Al Shora, Deputy Minister of Industry and Mineral Resources for Industrial Services and Compliance, and is hosting more than 1,000 exhibitors from over 50 countries against an organiser expectation of 35,000 or more trade visitors, under the theme from foundation to future, built for every scale.

Four co-located events are running alongside the main halls — Heavy Saudi Arabia, Totally Concrete Saudi Arabia, HVACR Saudi Arabia and Saudi FM & Clean.

The show's Impact Trail awards, announced across the event, went to three companies. Prime Middle East Trading Company, trading as PRIMECO, took Sustainability Innovation for its Solstice low global warming potential refrigerant solutions. Masdar won Best Circular Economy Solution for Kronospan products. Al-Futtaim Engineering Company won Operational Sustainability for its integrated facilities management offering. The Impact Trail also spotlighted solutions from Galaxy Technology, which is showing the Albion Valves range with carbon transparency data across its cast-iron products, Star Factory with spray polyurethane foam roofing and waterproofing, and Keller with ground improvement and foundation solutions.

The award categories are a fair reading of where the Saudi market's attention has moved. Refrigerant transition matters in a country whose peak electrical load is cooling. Circular economy claims about building materials are being tested against procurement policies rather than treated as marketing. And operational sustainability — the efficiency of an asset once it is running — is the category that matters most for a country about to own a very large quantity of new buildings.

The conference programme is organised around codes, standards and regulations, health and safety, sustainability, artificial intelligence, technology, project management, concrete, modular construction and HVACR. Sessions address navigating the Saudi Building Code, improving concrete quality, strengthening project governance, applying artificial intelligence in project delivery, and improving coordination between HVACR design, installation and facilities management. That final topic is a precise description of a recurring failure mode: a system designed by one party, installed by a second, commissioned by a third and operated by a fourth, with the performance data rarely surviving any of the handovers.

Speaking organisations include Dussman Ajlan & Bros, the Saudi Building Code Center, ROSHN Group, SEVEN, Al Kholi Group, Saudi Binladin Group, Modern Building Leaders, Misk City and Kabbani Construction Group. Christopher Seymour, managing director for the Middle East and Africa at Mace Consult, and Shonagh Kinnaird, project director at Misk City, are among the named speakers, with sessions examining collaboration between stakeholders, digital transparency, procurement challenges and lessons drawn from the Kingdom's major developments.

The exhibitor mix runs from established Saudi and regional names — Masdar, Al Yamamah Steel Industries with structural steel, CPC Holding, Lanmix, Al Muqarram — through to international suppliers including Schüco, Hempel, Alumil, Antolini, Elite Stone, CITCO, Coastal Qatar and White Helmet. Machinery and technology occupy an unusually large share of the floor for a construction show, from reinforcement processing plant through construction robotics to connected monitoring systems.

Two days remain, closing on 2 September. The through-line of day two was that the questions being asked of exhibitors have narrowed and hardened: can it be delivered on the date, can its performance be proved against a test regime, can it be supported inside the Kingdom, and what does it cost to run for the next thirty years. Those are the criteria the award categories reward, and they are the criteria on which most of this floor will now be judged.

The one thing the halls could not answer is the question underneath the whole pipeline. Saudi Arabia's construction workforce exceeded 3.4 million at the end of 2025 and the sector is carrying a shortage of skilled and specialist roles running into the hundreds of thousands, with technical positions taking three to six months to fill. Almost every technology on this floor is sold as a partial answer to that shortage. None of them removes the need for the qualified people who specify, install, commission and maintain what is being bought.
author: BrentDesk Staff
